incident: 2022 Pakistan monsoon floods (Sindh, Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, South Punjab)
dates: 14 June - October 2022 (peak July-August; national emergency declared 25 August 2022; some areas inundated for months)

basics.deaths: PDNA/World Bank: "More than 1730 lost their lives"; NDMA: 1,735 killed and 12,867 injured as of 28 Oct 2022; Munich Re: 'At least 1,700'; figure of 1,739 commonly cited later
basics.displaced: 7.9 million displaced; ~598,000 in relief camps (OCHA, 23 Sep 2022); final OCHA report cites at least 664,000 in camps and informal sites
basics.damage_usd: "Total damages to exceed USD 14.9 billion, and total economic losses to reach about USD 15.2 billion"; reconstruction needs "at least USD 16.3 billion" (PDNA, 28 Oct 2022). Sindh ~70% of damages and losses.
basics.insured_share: Munich Re: "Almost nothing was insured" (direct losses at least US$15bn)
basics.rainfall: PMD (via Aaj News, 6 Sep 2022): national August rainfall 243% above average, Sindh +726%, Balochistan +590%; August 2022 rain alone exceeded the normal whole-monsoon total by 37%; Padidan (Sindh) 355.0 mm on 19 Aug

I01_governing_party_and_help.finding: Relief flows were visibly politicised along federal (PDM coalition led by PML-N, with PPP) vs PTI-run provinces (KP, and Punjab at the time) lines. Pakistan Today (15 Sep 2022) reported the Finance Ministry began transferring "Rs15 billion to Sindh and Rs10 billion to Balochistan in the head of flood grants", while "in the case of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Gilgit-Baltistan, it would be disbursed to flood affectee through federal government's departments like the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA)" (headline: 'Centre playing politics with grants release to KP, GB flood affectees'; based on unnamed finance-division sources). In parallel, PTI ran its own telethon (29 Aug 2022, >Rs5bn pledged), with money routed to "the official accounts of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Punjab governments"; Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal questioned it. Imran Khan kept holding rallies ('Rallies will be held in floods, even wars'), which the government criticised.
I01_governing_party_and_help.value: Direct provincial grants: Sindh Rs15bn, Balochistan Rs10bn; KP/GB routed via NDMA instead

I02_election_effect.finding: No systematic study found linking 2022 flood exposure to Feb 2024 results. Descriptively, the PPP (governing Sindh, the worst-hit province) faced "criticism of his party's governance of Sindh for the past four terms, especially after cataclysmic 2022 flooding, which destroyed much of the province" (Al Jazeera), yet won a record 84 general seats in the Sindh Assembly on 8 Feb 2024. Flood housing (2.1 million houses with ownership rights) featured in Bilawal Bhutto Zardari's campaign. No evidence of an electoral penalty for the incumbent in flood-hit Sindh.
I02_election_effect.value: PPP 84 general Sindh Assembly seats (2024), its best result since 2008

I03_election_timing_and_visits.finding: PM Shehbaz Sharif visited flood-hit Jhal Magsi (Nasirabad division, Balochistan) on 31 July 2022, promising "Rs1 million to families of each victim" from federal and provincial governments each; later visited Sukkur and Jaffarabad (Rs10bn grant for Balochistan) and did aerial surveys of Sindh/Balochistan. UN Secretary-General Guterres visited Sukkur, Usta Muhammad, Mohenjo-Daro and Karachi on 9-10 Sep 2022. Elections were disrupted: the ECP decided to "indefinitely postpone the by-elections in at least 10 National Assembly constituencies and three provincial assembly seats" scheduled 11 Sep-2 Oct 2022, citing "floods and the unavailability of military and paramilitary personnel"; the Sindh local-government second phase (Karachi/Hyderabad divisions) was postponed repeatedly from July/August 2022 due to rain and floods. The general election was held 8 Feb 2024, about 18 months after the floods.
I03_election_timing_and_visits.value: First PM visit 31 Jul 2022; by-polls postponed Sep 2022; general election Feb 2024

I04_declaration_threshold_and_funds.finding: Federal government declared a national emergency on 25 Aug 2022 and deployed the military. Federal cash relief: BISP Flood Relief Cash Assistance, Rs25,000 per family, target Rs70bn for 2.7 million families; by 25 Oct 2022 BISP had paid "66,585,950,000 among 2,663,438 flood-affected families" (~97.3%) -- i.e. most paid within ~2 months. UN flash appeal revised to US$816m (UNICEF share US$173.5m, only 13% funded as of 7 Oct 2022). Geneva conference (9 Jan 2023) raised about US$10-10.9bn in pledges (Express Tribune reported $10.7bn), but Dawn reported "$8.7bn are loans" with ~$1.3bn grants; Islamic Relief said a year later "Almost 90% of the pledges came in the form of long-term loans" and most had not reached people.
I04_declaration_threshold_and_funds.value: BISP Rs66.6bn to 2.66m families by 25 Oct 2022; Geneva pledges ~US$10bn, ~87-90% loans

I05_infrastructure_repair_and_accountabi.finding: PDNA: Transport and Communications damage USD 3.3 billion (third-largest sector). About 13,115 km of roads and 439 bridges damaged (Wikipedia compilation of NDMA data). Accountability case: an investigation into the 2022 flood relief fund in Upper Dir (KP) found rampant embezzlement, with 40 approved steel bridges never built (Express Tribune, 'Flood relief scandal: 40 bridges never built'). No systematic data found on % of roads/bridges repaired.
I05_infrastructure_repair_and_accountabi.value: Transport damage USD 3.3bn; 13,115 km roads, 439 bridges damaged; 40 'ghost' bridges in Upper Dir

I06_health_facility_disruption.finding: "Over 1460 healthcare facilities have been damaged in Pakistan since June" 2022 (Alied et al., Annals of Medicine and Surgery, 2023). UNFPA (30 Aug 2022): over 1,000 health facilities partially or fully damaged in Sindh and 198 in affected Balochistan districts. WHO reported ~10% of health facilities nationally damaged or destroyed (Oct 2022, cited by East Asia Forum). PDNA health-sector damage estimated at about USD 109 million.

I07_birth_or_maternal_outcomes.finding: UNFPA (30 Aug 2022): "almost 650,000 pregnant women in the flood-affected areas require maternal" health services; "Up to 73,000 women expected to deliver next month will need skilled birth" attendants and newborn care. UNFPA (21 Sep 2022): "Nearly 130,000 pregnant women in need of urgent health services", "more than 42,000 of whom are due to give birth in the next three months". No population-level data found on actual birth outcomes (stillbirth, low birth weight, maternal deaths) attributable to the floods.
I07_birth_or_maternal_outcomes.value: ~650,000 pregnant women affected; 73,000 births expected within a month

I08_waterborne_disease.finding: Malaria: WHO/UN reported over 540,000 malaria cases July-early Oct 2022 in flood-affected areas; Sindh August cases rose from 19,826 (Aug 2021) to 69,123 (Aug 2022) and high-burden districts from 178,657 (Aug 2022) to 389,372 (Sep 2022) (Tabassum et al., Health Science Reports 2023). Dengue: 25,932 confirmed cases and 62 deaths nationally 1 Jan-27 Sep 2022 (WHO DON414). Diarrhoea/skin: "534 800" people treated for diarrhoea and "594 241" for skin illnesses at Sindh medical camps (Alied et al. 2023). Cholera and typhoid also reported. WHO warned of a 'second disaster'.
I08_waterborne_disease.value: >540,000 malaria cases (Jul-Oct 2022); 25,932 dengue cases; ~534,800 diarrhoea treatments in Sindh camps

I09_displacement_shelter_and_mental_heal.finding: 7.9 million displaced, of whom ~598,000 were in relief camps (OCHA, 23 Sep 2022). More than a year later IOM reported over 1.3 million people still displaced in the 30 worst-affected districts. An IGC survey of 5,100 rural Sindh households found "Only 41% of households evacuated", floods lasted on average 74 days with 24 days of displacement, and 56% stayed to guard house/land. Mental health: a Hyderabad (Sindh) study reported depression 68%, anxiety 62%, PTSD 55% among flood-affected respondents (International Journal of Asian Education and Psychology; small non-representative sample); Islamic Relief (Jan 2024) quoted a Sindh villager: "five people have committed suicide in the past year".
I09_displacement_shelter_and_mental_heal.value: 7.9m displaced; ~598k in camps; 1.3m still displaced >1 year later

I10_child_deaths_and_timing.finding: UNICEF (Oct 2022): "Pakistan's catastrophic floods have already claimed the lives of 615 children" (615 children killed 14 Jun-28 Sep; 4,006 injured). Early September reporting (CNN, 4 Sep 2022) said about a third of the ~1,280 dead were children; Avoidable Deaths Network: "children account for over a third of total deaths". Final NDMA count commonly cited as 647 children of ~1,739 deaths (~37%). Children also faced follow-on risks: UNICEF estimated over half a million children with severe acute malnutrition; later screening found >1 in 9 children in flood areas with SAM.

I11_property_value_effects.finding: No study or official data found on land or property value changes in flood-affected areas after the 2022 floods.

I12_recovery_speed_nightlights_or_rebuil.finding: Night lights: a NASA Black Marble study of the Indus flood found radiance in flooded areas was affected for ~13 weeks, fell by a factor of ~5 at the main flood, and took ~10 weeks after flooding to recover to pre-flood levels, with uneven recovery across socio-economic groups (ESS Open Archive preprint). Housing: Islamic Relief (Jan 2024) found "only around 5% of flood-damaged homes rebuilt" a year after Geneva. Sindh People's Housing for Flood Affectees (2.1m-house programme): by June 2024 over 100,000 houses completed and 525,000 under construction (Dawn); Amnesty (Oct 2024) cites 100,000 completed and 500,000 under construction. World Bank says its Sindh housing project supported over 410,000 core housing units.
I12_recovery_speed_nightlights_or_rebuil.value: Night lights recovered ~10 weeks after flooding; ~5% of 2.1m damaged homes fully rebuilt by Jan 2024

I13_income_employment_loss.finding: PDNA: "A total of 4.3 million workers across all provinces have been affected"; agriculture and livestock damage USD 3.7 billion; GDP loss "around 2.2 percent of FY22 GDP"; national poverty could rise 3.7-4.0 percentage points, "pushing between 8.4 and 9.1 million more people below the poverty line". ILO (28 Sep 2022): "2.36 to 3.6 million jobs may have been lost and/or disrupted". Satellite assessment of Sindh: expected production losses of 88% for cotton, 80% for rice, 61% for sugarcane; combined crop and livestock loss ~USD 1.7bn in Sindh. PDNA notes women lost agricultural/livestock livelihoods.
I13_income_employment_loss.value: 4.3m workers affected; 8.4-9.1m pushed into poverty; GDP -2.2%

I14_relief_grants_uptake.finding: BISP flood cash (Rs25,000/family) reached 2,663,438 families (Rs66.59bn, 97.3% of Rs70bn target) by 25 Oct 2022; Sindh 1,820,504 families, Punjab 325,432, KP 302,454, Balochistan 214,582, GB 466. Coverage limits: Humanitarian Outcomes reported that only 2.76 million of the over 8 million existing BISP beneficiary families living in flood-affected areas received payments, and the programme did not cover people newly impoverished by the floods. Sindh housing programme: ~1.02 million families had received financial support by Aug 2025 (reported by UrduPoint).
I14_relief_grants_uptake.value: 2.66m families paid Rs25,000 (97.3% of target) within ~2 months

I15_insured_vs_uninsured.finding: Munich Re NatCatSERVICE: "Direct losses are estimated to be at least US$ 15bn" and "Almost nothing was insured". Pakistan's insurance penetration is about 1% and crop insurance has little reach (Express Tribune commentary). No study found comparing recovery of insured vs uninsured households.

I16_observation_radar_forecast_quality.finding: Forecast skill was good at the meteorological level: Malik et al. (Environmental Research: Climate, 2023) found "the extreme precipitation during 17-18 August 2022 was predictable a week before the event"; all models captured it at a 6-day lead time, with UKMO/ECMWF hit rates above 0.5 up to 5 days ahead. ECMWF reported signals of severe flooding up to 3 weeks ahead in extended-range forecasts. Observation gaps: PMD runs only a few weather radars (Islamabad, Karachi, Mardan, Sialkot as of 2026, with Multan being added with JICA support) (radar ranges: S-band ~450 km, X-band Mardan ~120 km, C-band Sialkot ~350 km; INP, 2026); weak mountain monitoring and slow data sharing between provinces were also reported.
I16_observation_radar_forecast_quality.value: Extreme rain predictable ~6 days ahead; ~4 operational PMD radars

I17_community_warning_systems.finding: Last-mile warning was weak. UNESCO review: communities experienced "zero effective lead time" in 2022 (and 2025) even when forecasts existed, and recommended impact-based forecasting, local 'human sensors', sirens, mosque loudspeakers and radio. A Frontiers in Earth Science (2023) review of Pakistan's flood EWS found "77% of respondents saw a lack of coordination between producers and consumers as a significant obstacle", that many at risk did not take warnings seriously, and that "Nearly 90% of the project budget is allocated" to monitoring/warning technology rather than community components. IGC survey in rural Sindh: "Only 41% of households evacuated", many staying to guard land (76% lacked a formal title deed), so warnings alone would not have moved people.
I17_community_warning_systems.value: 'Zero effective lead time'; 41% of surveyed Sindh households evacuated

I18_power_telecom_outage_during_warning.finding: On 26 Aug 2022 telephone and internet services were cut in 10 Balochistan districts (Quetta, Ziarat, Khuzdar, Loralai, Pishin, Chaman, Panjgur, Zhob, Qila Saifullah, Qila Abdullah) after the PTA cited "a serious damage to the cable and optical-fibre network due to torrential rains and flash floods"; PTCL fibre was cut in three places; services were partly restored within hours via bypass and satellite links. The Nation reported internet services suspended in 80% of Balochistan (31 Aug 2022). UNESCO notes GSM, electricity and internet "frequently fail during severe weather events", limiting SMS alerts.
I18_power_telecom_outage_during_warning.value: 10 Balochistan districts lost phone/internet on 26 Aug 2022

I19_warning_language_and_accessibility.finding: No 2022-specific evidence found on which languages (Urdu/English vs Sindhi, Balochi, Saraiki, Pashto) warnings were issued in, or on reach among non-Urdu speakers. General evidence on Pakistan's EWS (Frontiers 2023, citing Shah et al. 2022): "Official early warning system uses technical language, making it harder for at-risk populations to comprehend", and women are excluded or only partly included in preparedness activities. UNESCO recommends warnings be "translated into localized and actionable guidance for communities".

I20_warning_system_design_change_after.finding: Post-2022 changes: the Resilient Recovery, Rehabilitation and Reconstruction Framework (4RF, launched 21 Dec 2022; US$16.26bn of interventions) set out the recovery and resilience plan; NDMA revamped its National Emergencies Operation Centre (NEOC), which PM Shehbaz Sharif visited on 21 Jun 2024, with "multiple satellite feeds, software and artificial intelligence tools" and a claimed "capability to forecast weather six to ten months in advance"; NDMA launched a disaster-alert mobile app (Pak NDMA Disaster Alert); PMD is adding radars (Multan, JICA-supported). No independent evaluation found showing improved last-mile warning; the UNESCO review says 'zero effective lead time' recurred in 2025.
I20_warning_system_design_change_after.value: NEOC revamped (2024); 4RF (Dec 2022); new radar under installation

who_died: About 46% of the 1,735 deaths (NDMA, 28 Oct 2022) were in Sindh, 19% in Balochistan, 18% in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and 13% in Punjab (as summarised from NDMA/CRS). By late September the counts were Sindh 724, KP 306, Balochistan 304 (Avoidable Deaths Network, 28 Sep 2022, https://www.avoidable-deaths.net/2022/09/28/rapid-review-of-flood-damage-and-loss-in-pakistan/). Children were over a third of the dead: 615 by late September (UNICEF), and 647 in the final count. Deaths were concentrated in the alluvial Indus plains with many rural poor people (Avoidable Deaths Network), plus flash floods in Balochistan and in the KP mountains (e.g. Swat). No NDMA breakdown of 2022 causes of death (house collapse vs drowning vs electrocution) was found. Note: the widely quoted 'two-thirds from house collapses and flash floods' figure is from the 2025 monsoon, not 2022 (Al Jazeera, Jul 2025). In one household survey, 95% of surveyed rural Sindh households reported housing damage and about half had homes fully washed away (IGC). Excess deaths from disease and malnutrition after the flood are not counted.
blame_framing: The dominant official and international framing was climate change and climate injustice. UN Secretary-General Guterres (10 Sep 2022): "I have never seen climate carnage on this scale", adding that "G20 countries are responsible for 80 per cent of today's emissions" and "Wealthier countries are morally responsible for helping developing countries like Pakistan" (https://news.un.org/en/story/2022/09/1126411). World Weather Attribution (14 Sep 2022) found climate change "could have increased the rainfall intensity up to 50%" for the 5-day event, but also blamed the "proximity of human settlements ... to flood plains, inadequate infrastructure, limited ex-ante risk reduction capacity, an outdated river management system" and poverty (https://www.worldweatherattribution.org/climate-change-likely-increased-extreme-monsoon-rainfall-flooding-highly-vulnerable-communities-in-pakistan/). Munich Re also pointed to climate change (~50% more intense). Domestically, the parties blamed each other: the federal government criticised Imran Khan's rallies during the floods and doubted his telethon (Ahsan Iqbal), and PTI accused the centre of politicising grants to KP/GB. There were also claims about local causes: farmers said powerful landowners controlled irrigation water (Foreign Policy, Nov 2022), and Amnesty (Oct 2024) accused the Sindh government of failing to fulfil rights to healthcare, food and housing after the floods. Warning failure was a secondary theme, mostly raised by researchers and NGOs ('zero effective lead time', UNESCO) rather than officials.
inquiries_and_consequences: No national judicial or parliamentary inquiry into flood deaths or warning failures was found, and no resignations of ministers or officials over the 2022 flood response were found. What did happen: the PDNA (Oct 2022) and the 4RF recovery framework (Dec 2022); the Geneva International Conference on Climate Resilient Pakistan (9 Jan 2023, ~US$10bn pledged, mostly loans); the Sindh People's Housing for Flood Affectees programme for 2.1m houses; a local corruption investigation in Upper Dir, KP, that found 40 flood-relief steel bridges were never built (Express Tribune); and the NDMA NEOC upgrade (2024). No prosecutions or convictions linked to flood deaths were found.
notes: Several primary sources (ReliefWeb, OCHA, UNDP, CRS, PDNA PDF) returned HTTP 403 or unreadable PDFs to the fetch tool; figures from them are taken from search-result extracts or from secondary pages quoting them (e.g. the World Bank PDNA press release was fetched directly). The WebSearch budget ran out mid-task, so some items (2022-specific causes of death, warning languages, property values, systematic road-repair progress) could not be searched further. Death totals vary slightly by date (1,717 / 1,730+ / 1,735 / 1,739). Rainfall anomalies: PMD monthly summary gives Sindh +726% and Balochistan +590% for August; the '784%' figure on Wikipedia is not used as primary. The Hyderabad mental-health prevalence figures come from a small local study and are not representative. For comparison with KZN 2022: Pakistan's scale is about 30-40 times larger in deaths and affected people, insurance was near zero, and the cash relief (BISP) reached ~2.66m families within about 2 months through an existing social-protection registry.
